title: Stop an approved automation from executing twice
summary: A small agency delivers an automation that sends invoices or changes records. After a timeout or approval pause, it repeats the action. Build a testable execution boundary that catches duplicate and changed requests before they reach the tool.
audience: Small automation agencies maintaining client workflows
buyer: Agency technical lead responsible for production incidents
flow: Compare approved intent and execution key
Block duplicate action + show an audit receipt
deliverable: A runnable simulated invoice workflow, protective adapter and failure-injection demo
question: Can an adapter prevent duplicate and stale-approved writes across retries, without blocking legitimate new requests?
measure: On a declared fixture suite: count duplicate writes, stale approvals accepted, legitimate actions blocked and adapter latency. No exactly-once claim for arbitrary external APIs.
baseline: Framework idempotent-task guidance, durable execution and API idempotency keys. These already solve parts of the problem.
proposed_difference: Package a narrow integration test and approval-to-action consistency check for client handover. Whether agencies need a separate product remains untested.
risk: Drop the product if the framework or destination API solves the entire workflow with a small configuration change, or agency users reject the added integration work.
data_plan: Synthetic invoice records and a fake side-effect API; reproduce the failure on pinned framework versions. No real payments or client systems.
model_plan: Deterministic state checks and idempotency storage; no model needed in the enforcement path.
why_ml: AI may initiate the workflow, but enforcing approved intent should be deterministic.
venture: Start as a reliability audit and integration service; a reusable regression suite could support recurring maintenance. Pricing and demand are hypotheses.
customer_test: Owner can show the failure demo to three automation maintainers and ask for an anonymised incident and a trial integration. No outreach is sent automatically.
week_test: Deliver replay controls, adapter, failure tests and before/after receipts in 3–5 days. Test whether a maintainer can integrate it into one sandbox workflow.
growth_path: One adapter → reusable client acceptance tests → maintained integrations and incident regression coverage.
evidence: Two practitioner reports describe replay/interrupt problems. They establish a failure pattern, not market size or willingness to pay. Verify current versions; reported bugs may be fixed.
evidence_level: Practitioner problem reports; purchasing demand untested

provenance.title: Practitioner report: pre-interrupt work repeats
provenance.finding: A practitioner asks how to distinguish resume execution because pre-interrupt code runs again.

provenance.title: LangGraph issue #7780
provenance.finding: Reports repeated interrupt/resume behaviour in loops; reproduce before assuming the report applies to a current release.

provenance.title: LangGraph interrupt reference
provenance.finding: Interrupt values are matched by order within a node. Framework semantics are a baseline, not our invention.

reason: Best first fit for software reliability and an AI-Org service: a reproducible operational failure, bounded scope and reachable practitioners.
contribution: A runnable simulated invoice workflow, protective adapter and failure-injection demo
feasibility: Laptop-first, small fixtures, no paid APIs or compute. Customer validation remains a separate owner-led step.
next: Deliver replay controls, adapter, failure tests and before/after receipts in 3–5 days. Test whether a maintainer can integrate it into one sandbox workflow.
originality: Not claimed novel. Sources establish the problem or existing methods; the proposed product gap and willingness to pay remain hypotheses.
alternative: Framework idempotent-task guidance, durable execution and API idempotency keys. These already solve parts of the problem.

title: Find the invoice mistakes that distort a restaurant’s food costs
summary: A restaurant receives supplier invoices with inconsistent descriptions, pack sizes and occasional extraction errors. Give the owner an exception inbox showing which cost changes need checking and the original evidence behind each flag.
audience: Independent restaurant operators and their bookkeepers
buyer: Owner or bookkeeper responsible for reconciling supplier costs
flow: Check duplicates, pack sizes and price changes
deliverable: An interactive invoice exception inbox with an auditable correction history
question: Can an exception-first review reduce checking time without hiding genuine invoice errors?
measure: Known-error recall, false flags per invoice and correction time against a spreadsheet on a clearly labelled fixture set; real usefulness requires an operator trial.
baseline: Mindee already extracts invoice line items; xtraCHEF already offers restaurant invoice automation. A generic OCR app would duplicate existing products.
proposed_difference: Test a lightweight, locally processed exception review for operators who cannot justify a full purchasing platform. This segment and gap are hypotheses.
risk: Stop if operators already solve this cheaply, cannot supply consented examples, or correction time exceeds spreadsheet review. Do not promise accounting accuracy.
data_plan: Week one: bundled synthetic invoices and editable extracted CSV/JSON. Later: consented, redacted Swedish supplier invoices; no scraping private documents.
model_plan: Rules for totals and duplicate rows; optional small pretrained text embeddings for product matching only after exact matching baseline. PDF OCR is a later extension.
why_ml: Matching varied supplier descriptions may benefit from embeddings; arithmetic and duplicate checks should use rules.
venture: Potential narrow food-operations product or managed onboarding service; recurring value would come from verified cost history, not one-off OCR.
customer_test: Owner can test the inbox with two local operators/bookkeepers and ask which flags change an actual purchasing or correction decision.
week_test: In 4–6 days build CSV import, seeded duplicate/pack-size cases, side-by-side source view, corrections and export. No bank/POS integration or automated supplier disputes.
growth_path: Exception inbox → supplier-specific matching learned from corrections → repeatable onboarding for small operators.
evidence: A vendor feedback report describes duplicated extracted rows (search-index evidence; full page fetch timed out). Vendor material describes line-item and restaurant review problems. These are biased, limited signals, not validated local demand.
evidence_level: User report + vendor evidence; local demand untested

provenance.title: Invoice user reports duplicate rows
provenance.finding: A user reports duplicated line-item extraction. Full-page verification failed; treat this as a lead, not a confirmed current product defect.

provenance.title: Mindee: invoice line-item extraction
provenance.finding: Explains table structure and extraction challenges and an existing commercial solution.

provenance.title: xtraCHEF restaurant AP guide
provenance.finding: Describes restaurant invoice review and unit/price visibility problems. Older vendor material; no market-size estimates are adopted.

reason: Connects food interests to a concrete operating decision, with a local route to customer learning.
contribution: An interactive invoice exception inbox with an auditable correction history

originality: Not claimed novel. Sources establish the problem or existing methods; the proposed product gap and willingness to pay remain hypotheses.
alternative: Mindee already extracts invoice line items; xtraCHEF already offers restaurant invoice automation. A generic OCR app would duplicate existing products.

title: Can this customer’s data support the model they want?
summary: Before quoting a custom visual model, an AI consultant needs to know whether the customer’s labels and examples can support the requested outcome. Build a customer-facing feasibility report that exposes label disagreements and the value of correcting them.
audience: Small consultancies adapting pretrained vision models for clients
buyer: Consultancy lead scoping a paid model pilot
flow: Import labelled images and target cost of errors
Review corrections + produce a go/no-go pilot brief
deliverable: A local visual-data audit and reproducible pilot feasibility report
question: Does reviewing suspect labels change the model choice or attainable error rate enough to affect a pilot decision?
measure: Held-out quality before/after a fixed review budget, review precision, runtime and changed go/no-go decisions. Keep the final test set untouched.
baseline: Cleanlab already identifies potential label errors; pretrained features and simple classifiers already support small-data baselines.
proposed_difference: Test a service deliverable linking evidence quality, review effort and customer error costs to a pilot decision. This is packaging and evaluation, not a new label-cleaning algorithm.
risk: Exploratory: no specific buyer complaint has been verified. Stop if consultants already produce the report easily or no customer will share suitable labelled data.
data_plan: Small licensed visual subset with known seeded label errors, documented provenance and held-out split. No claim that public data represents a client.
model_plan: Cached pretrained image embeddings + linear classifier; compare simple baseline and existing label-quality tooling. No GPU training required for the first slice.
why_ml: This tests whether adapting a pretrained model is viable for a customer rather than assuming it is worth building.
venture: A paid feasibility audit could lead to customer-specific model adaptation and monitoring contracts; demand must be established before expanding.
customer_test: First obtain feedback from a consultant on whether the report changes a real quotation or pilot decision. Stronger evidence is required before automatic build selection.
week_test: In 3–5 days produce one local image-label review journey, frozen test split, before/after comparison and exportable client brief. First milestone: inspect data/licence and baseline runtime.
growth_path: Feasibility audit → bounded model adaptation pilot → measured maintenance under data changes.
evidence: Published research establishes that label errors can change model rankings; Cleanlab is an established alternative. Neither establishes that this consultancy report is a missing product.
evidence_level: Research evidence only; customer pain unverified
market: Exploratory; not eligible for default build

provenance.title: Label errors can change model rankings
provenance.finding: Studies label errors across ten benchmark test sets and their effect on model comparisons. It does not establish a buyer for our proposed service.

provenance.title: Cleanlab existing tooling
provenance.finding: Provides established data-quality and label-error tooling; our work must compare against it rather than rebrand it.

reason: Directly explores a custom-model business, with an explicit evidence gap rather than presenting a tutorial as an opportunity.
contribution: A local visual-data audit and reproducible pilot feasibility report
feasibility: Laptop-first, small fixtures, no paid APIs or compute. Customer validation remains a separate owner-led step.
next: In 3–5 days produce one local image-label review journey, frozen test split, before/after comparison and exportable client brief. First milestone: inspect data/licence and baseline runtime.
originality: Not claimed novel. Sources establish the problem or existing methods; the proposed product gap and willingness to pay remain hypotheses.
alternative: Cleanlab already identifies potential label errors; pretrained features and simple classifiers already support small-data baselines.

title: Can a defect detector survive a change of lighting?
summary: Adapt pretrained visual features to a small inspection task, then test when lighting changes make the detector unreliable.
deliverable: A small-data robustness study with explicit failure boundaries
question: Does threshold calibration or limited adaptation improve reliability under lighting shift at a fixed false-alarm budget?
measure: Image-level AUROC, recall at fixed false-alarm rate, calibration, inference time; split by acquisition condition.
baseline: Frozen features + nearest-neighbour anomaly score; simple image statistics; an existing Anomalib baseline.
alternative: Frozen features + nearest-neighbour anomaly score; simple image statistics; an existing Anomalib baseline.
proposed_difference: A controlled comparison of adaptation and calibration under predefined lighting shifts and label budgets—not a recreation of the benchmark.
risk: Prior work may already answer the question; industrial images do not establish performance on a customer’s production line.
data_plan: Inspect one MVTec AD 2 public subset. Verify dataset terms before downloading; commercial reuse is not assumed.
model_plan: Pretrained vision backbone; frozen features first, a small adapter only if feasible.
why_ml: Visual variability is hard to encode with fixed thresholds, but simple statistics may still win.
venture: Possible service: adapt and validate inspection models on customer-owned images. No willingness-to-pay evidence yet.
contribution: A small-data robustness study with explicit failure boundaries
feasibility: Start with a small public-data feasibility check on the laptop. Record licences, memory and runtime before scaling; no paid compute.
next: Write a feasibility brief, verify closest papers, inspect data access and design a leakage-safe pilot. Do not conduct the full thesis.
reason: Fits task-specific applied AI; compare against simpler alternatives before committing.
evidence: Technical starting points are verified below. Customer interviews, commercial rights and novelty checks are still outstanding.

provenance.title: MVTec AD 2 benchmark
provenance.finding: Includes normal training images and test images under different lighting. This motivates a shift-robustness study, not a new anomaly-detection method.

provenance.title: Anomalib implementation library
provenance.finding: Existing anomaly-detection implementations and deployment tooling. Use as baselines; do not present library functionality as original work.

originality: Proposed adaptation/evaluation, not a new model architecture. The extension is a hypothesis; literature review must establish whether it is already answered.

title: Can a sound model recognise your machine in a noisy room?
summary: Use pretrained audio features and a small classifier; investigate transfer across microphones or recording environments.
flow: Evaluate on a different recording setup
deliverable: A transfer-learning feasibility study with leakage-safe splits
question: How does a frozen audio representation compare with acoustic features when the recording environment changes?
measure: Macro F1, per-class recall, unseen-condition error and CPU latency; never split overlapping clips across train and test.
baseline: MFCC features + logistic regression; frozen YAMNet embeddings + linear head.
alternative: MFCC features + logistic regression; frozen YAMNet embeddings + linear head.
proposed_difference: Compare label budgets and recording-condition transfer for one accessible task; the tutorial’s training pipeline is prior work.
risk: Without recording-condition metadata, a claimed domain-shift study may be invalid. Environmental recognition is not fault diagnosis.
data_plan: First find a suitably licensed audio dataset with device/session metadata; if unavailable, narrow the question before committing.
model_plan: YAMNet embeddings with a small supervised head; no speech LLM.
why_ml: A small acoustic model can map sound patterns to bounded labels; a fixed amplitude threshold is the minimum baseline.
audience: Equipment-service teams or consumer device builders
venture: Possible customer-specific sound recognition service; need an actual use case and acceptable false-alarm cost.
contribution: A transfer-learning feasibility study with leakage-safe splits
feasibility: Start with a small public-data feasibility check on the laptop. Record licences, memory and runtime before scaling; no paid compute.

title: When does a pretrained forecast beat a simple local model?
summary: Compare pretrained forecasting with small locally trained models when each business has only a short history.
deliverable: A data-budget and transfer study for one forecasting task
question: Under what history length and shift conditions does a pretrained forecaster outperform seasonal and tabular baselines?
measure: Rolling-origin MASE/MAE, interval coverage, inference cost; hold out both future time and entities where possible.
baseline: Seasonal naive; moving average; gradient boosting with lag features; frozen Chronos baseline.
alternative: Seasonal naive; moving average; gradient boosting with lag features; frozen Chronos baseline.
proposed_difference: A preregistered comparison across history budgets and unseen entities, with compute-normalised results. A novelty check is required.
risk: Public retail data may poorly represent a small restaurant; pretrained training-data overlap must be investigated.
data_plan: Find an accessible demand dataset with entity and time identifiers; check licence and any pretrained overlap before finalising the study.
model_plan: Small Chronos variant if local resources permit; task-specific lag-feature model as a serious competitor.
why_ml: Demand has repeatable temporal structure; complex models must justify themselves against seasonal averages.
venture: Possible tailored forecasting and monitoring service. Savings and customer willingness to share sales data remain untested.
contribution: A data-budget and transfer study for one forecasting task
feasibility: Start with a small public-data feasibility check on the laptop. Record licences, memory and runtime before scaling; no paid compute.

title: Which examples are worth asking a business to label?
summary: Study how to choose training examples when expert labels are expensive and the model must work on a new customer’s data.
flow: Compare learning at equal label cost
deliverable: A bounded active-learning evaluation on one task
question: Does uncertainty-based sampling outperform random selection once class imbalance and domain shift are controlled?
measure: Performance versus label budget, minority recall and annotation effort; multiple seeds and a fixed untouched test set.
baseline: Random sampling and class-balanced sampling using the same frozen representation and classifier.
alternative: Random sampling and class-balanced sampling using the same frozen representation and classifier.
proposed_difference: Study when a simple selection policy fails or helps under explicit label costs; do not claim a new active-learning algorithm.
risk: A generic benchmark reproduction is insufficient for a thesis; a concrete task and literature gap must be established.
data_plan: Reuse one feasible vision or sound dataset after checking labels, split design and permitted use.
model_plan: Frozen pretrained features plus compact classifier; simple uncertainty sampling.
why_ml: ML can prioritise ambiguous samples, but random or balanced sampling may be equally effective.
audience: Businesses with limited expert labelling time
venture: Possible model-customisation service with efficient data collection. Demand and annotation costs need customer evidence.
contribution: A bounded active-learning evaluation on one task
feasibility: Start with a small public-data feasibility check on the laptop. Record licences, memory and runtime before scaling; no paid compute.
